Issue 1284: don't let a bucket lookup invent a key

bucket._cache was a defaultdict(deque), and _get_values opened with
`if self._cache[value]:` — a read that inserts an empty deque on a miss.
__iter__ reports `iter(self._cache)`, so every failed lookup left a
permanent phantom key behind, and __contains__ routes through
_get_values, so a plain `in` test was enough to create one.

The result was that `'c' in s` and `'c' in list(s)` disagreed for the
same object at the same moment, misses accumulated, and the docstring's
own "Get the keys" example returned a fourth key after one membership
test.

Make _cache a plain dict so a lookup cannot insert, and register a key
only where an item with that key is actually seen. A key whose items are
produced straight to the caller is registered at that point, so the
existing test_list case — a key fully consumed through s[key] is still
listed — keeps working.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Run them with: {python} -m pytest -q tests/test_more.py

Fix one()/only() dropping a falsy user-supplied exception

`one(it, too_long=exc)` and `only(it, too_long=exc)` used
`raise too_long or ValueError(msg)`, so a `too_long`/`too_short` whose
instances are falsy (e.g. an Exception subclass overriding `__bool__`)
was discarded and the default `ValueError` raised instead.

Switch to explicit `is not None` checks, and only build the default
message when no custom exception is supplied so a faulty `__repr__` on
the iterable's items can't shadow the requested exception.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Do not yield an empty list for an empty iterable when maxsplit is 0

split_before, split_after and split_when share a maxsplit == 0 fast path
that yields list(iterable) unconditionally, so an empty iterable produced
[[]] while every other maxsplit produced []. Their slow paths return
nothing for an empty iterable - split_before and split_after via 'if buf',
split_when via its StopIteration early return - and test_empty_collection
and test_empty_iterable already pin that, but neither passed maxsplit, so
neither reached the fast path.

split_at is left alone: its slow path yields the trailing empty list, which
matches ''.split(',', 0) == [''].

Don't mask TypeError raised while iterating in value_chain

value_chain used `yield from value` inside a `try/except TypeError`
guard. Because `yield from` consumes lazily, the guard stayed active
for the whole consumption rather than only classifying the argument,
so a TypeError raised from inside the argument was swallowed and the
partially-consumed object was emitted after the items it had already
produced:

    >>> list(value_chain(map(len, ['ab', 'cde', 5])))
    [2, 3, <map object at 0x...>]

Classify the argument with iter() and consume it outside the guard.
Arguments that cannot be iterated at all are still emitted as-is.

Issue 1247: Keep numeric_range consistent with the items it produces

numeric_range produces its items by repeated multiplication, but derived
len(), __contains__ and index() from division by the step. With floats the
two disagree, so a range could report a length that did not match what it
yielded, and could deny membership to its own items.

Settle all of them against the items themselves: _len trims or extends the
divided count until it matches the values produced, and index() confirms
the candidate position by comparing against the item at that position.
__contains__ and count() now follow index(), so the four cannot drift apart
again.

Exact types are unaffected: their remainders are already zero, so they take
the same path and the same number of operations as before.

Raise for negative slice sizes in sliced()

sliced(seq, n) with a negative n silently produced a wrong result
instead of raising or returning empty. Because the internal generator
uses seq[i : i + n] with i stepping by count(0, n), a negative n makes
takewhile(len, ...) yield a single truncated slice and stop:

    >>> list(sliced('ABCDEFG', -1))
    ['ABCDEF']

This is the worst failure mode: no error, just quietly incorrect
output. The documented sibling chunked() already rejects a negative n
(via islice), and tail() was recently changed to raise for negative
sizes for the same reason. sliced() is actually worse than pre-fix
tail(), which returned an empty result rather than wrong data.

Guard n < 0 up front and raise ValueError('n must be at least 0'),
matching tail()'s message. n == 0 still returns an empty iterator
(unchanged), as do all n >= 1 cases. With strict=True the negative
case previously raised a misleading "seq is not divisible by n"; it
now raises the correct domain error before iteration begins.

Add SlicedTests.test_negative covering both the default and strict
paths.

Support negative start/stop in iter_index for general iterables

iter_index has a fast path for objects with an .index method (str, list)
and a slow path for general iterables that uses islice. The fast path
accepts negative start/stop with the usual from-the-end semantics, but
the slow path crashed with 'Indices for islice() must be None or an
integer' because islice rejects negative indices, so the two paths
disagreed (the existing tests assert they agree for list and iter).

When start or stop is negative on the slow path, materialize the
iterable to a tuple and use its .index, matching the fast path. The
common non-negative path stays fully lazy.
